The Architecture of Hegemony: Beyond Distillation in the US-China AI Race

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s assertion that China is merely "copying homework" through model distillation fundamentally misdiagnoses the structural battlefield of artificial intelligence. 

Dismissing Chinese advancements as intellectual property parasitic on Western frontier labs misses the shift from theoretical algorithmic breakthroughs to industrial scale, deployment velocity, and sovereign vertical integration. 

While US firms battle over multi-billion-dollar cluster training costs, Beijing is constructing a hardened, full-stack techno-industrial ecosystem that connects physical raw inputs directly to mass-market operational systems.

China’s resilience begins at the atomic layer of the compute stack. Controlling over 65% of global rare earth mining and upwards of 85% to 90% of processing, Beijing holds critical leverage over materials essential for semiconductors, high-density server magnets, and advanced hardware. 

Despite severe US export restrictions on sub-7nm lithography tools from ASML, domestic champions led by Huawei and SMIC have engineered multi-patterning Deep Ultraviolet (DUV) processes alongside domestic lithography tooling. 

Domestically designed Ascend neural processing units (NPUs) have rapidly integrated across Chinese state data centers, ensuring that even if leading-edge TSMC silicon remains cut off, China maintains an uninterrupted domestic hardware floor capable of sustaining sovereign compute capacity.

Where the divergence becomes irreversible is in physical deployment. The United States maintains a dominant position in high-margin, cloud-based proprietary Large Language Models (LLMs) monetized via API tokens and enterprise seats. 

In contrast, China’s industrial strategy treats AI not as a distinct software layer, but as general-purpose infrastructure to be embedded into tangible production. China accounts for over 50% of global industrial robot installations and commands more than 60% of the world’s electric vehicle production. 

Companies like BYD, DJI, and Xiaomi integrate on-device neural processing, automated vision systems, and autonomous telemetry directly into millions of consumer and commercial endpoints annually. 

In the military domain, this industrial base supports autonomous swarming drones, electronic warfare automation, and sensor fusion, transforming algorithmic power into physical military-industrial capability.

Simultaneously, Chinese labs have weaponized the open-source software model to dismantle Silicon Valley’s proprietary moats. Open-weight architectures exemplified by DeepSeek, Alibaba’s Qwen series, https://t.co/zY06xloTpN, and Moonshot frequently trade parity blows with proprietary Western models on global evaluation benchmarks like MMLU and HumanEval, while requiring a fraction of the inference compute. 

By distributing these weights globally at near-zero marginal cost, Beijing has commoditized the core intelligence layer. This undercuts the premium subscription models of American tech giants, particularly across developing economies in Southeast Asia, Latin America, and the Middle East, which now build their domestic AI infrastructure atop Chinese open architectures.

Constrained domestic consumption forces these deeply automated, low-cost goods from algorithmic EVs to smart electronics onto the global market at hyper-competitive price points.

Washington’s escalating tariff regimes, entity listings, and outbound investment controls are not merely reactive measures against IP distillation; they represent a defensive effort against systemic industrial displacement. 

If the artificial intelligence revolution mirrors electrification rather than the software boom, victory will not belong solely to the lab that first conceptualized the current, but to the nation capable of wiring the global grid, mass-producing the appliances, and running the physical machinery of the modern economy.

[THE FACT] [Kang Il-hong’s Entertainment Today] ‘Kim Soo-hyun Investigation’ Finally Concluded: “Both the KakaoTalk Messages and Voice Recordings Were Fake”

Reporter: Kang Il-hong
Published: September 9, 2026, 12:37

“The KakaoTalk messages and the voice recordings were both fake.”

The investigation into the so-called “grooming of a minor” allegations that had followed Kim Soo-hyun for more than one year and four months has effectively reached its final conclusion. Attention is now focused on Kim Soo-hyun’s resumption of activities and the release date of Disney+’s Knock-Off, which is reportedly a large-scale production with a budget of approximately 60 billion won.

“The KakaoTalk messages and the voice recordings were fake.” The investigation into the so-called “grooming of a minor” allegations that had followed Kim Soo-hyun for more than one year and four months has effectively reached its final conclusion. After police decided not to forward the case due to no charges being established, the prosecution also returned the case records to the police without requesting additional or renewed investigation.

Now, there is only one major question: Kim Soo-hyun’s return to activities and the release of Disney+’s Knock-Off, reportedly made with a production budget of approximately 60 billion won.

On September 3, the Seoul Eastern District Prosecutors’ Office returned the records concerning the complaint against Kim Soo-hyun for violation of the Child Welfare Act and false accusation to Seongdong Police Station without requesting supplementary investigation. Previously, on July 29, police decided not to forward the case after determining that there was insufficient evidence to substantiate the allegations.

Particularly noteworthy in this investigation is the authenticity of the materials that were presented as the key evidence supporting the allegations. Police reportedly reviewed statements and materials from Kim Soo-hyun’s side, the bereaved family’s side, and other relevant individuals. They reportedly determined that some of the publicly released voice recordings had been manipulated using generative AI, while the KakaoTalk conversation screenshots were also fabricated materials that distorted actual conversations.

Ultimately, police concluded that it was difficult to establish the allegations concerning a relationship while Kim Sae-ron was a minor and the alleged grooming. The prosecution likewise did not request a reinvestigation. From Kim Soo-hyun’s perspective, this means he has, at least for now, escaped the biggest criminal-legal risk that had followed him for more than a year.

But the important thing is that this is not where the story ends. Signs of Kim Soo-hyun’s comeback have already begun.

Last month, he resumed overseas activities by appearing as a special guest on Indonesia’s RCTI 37th-anniversary special live broadcast. And on September 19, he is scheduled to attend the 2026 The Fact Music Awards (TMA) at Busan Asiad Main Stadium as a presenter.

This will mark his first official domestic public appearance in approximately one year and six months since his press conference last March. With signs of a resumption of advertising activities also emerging, the atmosphere is clearly changing.

There has also recently been a favorable court ruling for Kim Soo-hyun’s side in an advertising-contract dispute. The Seoul Eastern District Court rejected Swiss watch brand Mido’s claim seeking the return of approximately 570 million won in advertising contract payments from Kim Soo-hyun’s agency, Gold Medalist. In other words, following the conclusion of the criminal investigation, there has also been a positive development for Kim Soo-hyun in the civil arena.

Naturally, the attention of the industry and fans is now turning toward Knock-Off.

Knock-Off is a Disney+ original series about an ordinary office worker whose life is turned upside down by the 1997 Asian financial crisis and who eventually rises to become the king of the global counterfeit-goods market.

Kim Soo-hyun and Jo Bo-ah are the lead actors, and the production budget is reportedly around 60 billion won. The problem is that the drama had originally been preparing for release, but following the controversy surrounding Kim Soo-hyun, its release was indefinitely put on hold. With such a large-scale production, into which 60 billion won has reportedly been invested, effectively sitting on the sidelines, the situation is certainly not a minor issue for the production company or platform.

Of course, Disney+ has not officially announced a specific release date for Knock-Off. In fact, the platform previously denied reports that it was preparing to release the series this year. Therefore, it is not possible to state a release date with certainty at this point.

However, the situation itself has clearly changed.

Kim Soo-hyun has resumed overseas activities, is returning to official domestic events, police have decided not to forward the case, the prosecution has not requested supplementary investigation, and there has been a favorable initial ruling in the civil lawsuit concerning the advertising contract. The various factors that had been blocking the release are gradually being resolved one by one.

So the remaining question is this:

“When will the 60-billion-won Knock-Off finally open its doors?”

There is still no official announcement from Disney+. But at least now, with the criminal investigation surrounding Kim Soo-hyun effectively concluded and the actor himself resuming both domestic and overseas activities, the situation is completely different from before.

Ultimately, the question of Knock-Off’s release has moved beyond Kim Soo-hyun’s personal comeback. It has become a question of when a major piece of content that has already received a massive production investment should be brought to the market.

It may have been a long and painful period for Kim Soo-hyun, but the industry's focus is now shifting away from “Can he make a comeback?” toward “When will Knock-Off, the first major project of his comeback, be released?”

The 60-billion-won door is still closed. But now there are far more reasons to open it than there were before.

🇳🇴 Bergen, Norway

Department: Faculty of Psychology, SLATE, AI LEARN Centre (Ethics, Governance and Regulation cluster)
Supervisors: Dr. Anja Salzmann (UiB), Prof. Wayne Holmes (UCL)
Deadline: September 29, 2026
Duration: 3 years
Salary: NOK 593,700/year

📋 About the Project
AI LEARN is a new national Norwegian center focused on empowering human learning through responsible, human-centered AI, bringing together 31 national and international academic, public, and private sector partners to study hybrid intelligence — humans and machines learning and working together. This PhD sits within the Ethics, Governance and Regulation cluster, investigating ethical issues (human dignity, social justice, human agency, human flourishing) raised by AI — including generative AI — across learning contexts like K-12, informal/formal training, and vocational or professional development. The student will conduct qualitative empirical research grounded in relevant theory to inform ethical frameworks for policy, professional development, curriculum design, and pedagogy.

🔬 Ideal Candidate
• Master's degree in Social Sciences, Education, Science and Technology Studies (STS), Philosophy, or related field
• Grade B or higher on master's thesis (or equivalent average grade)
• Demonstrated interest in AI ethics in learning contexts is an advantage
• Strong independent and structured working style, good collaboration skills
• Excellent written and spoken English

✨ Why Apply
Join a genuinely interdisciplinary, well-resourced national center at the frontier of AI ethics and education, co-supervised across Bergen and UCL. UiB offers strong benefits including membership in the Norwegian Public Service Pension Fund and competitive state salary scale conditions.

📍 Bergen is a scenic coastal Norwegian city with a strong academic tradition and growing AI/tech research focus.

Elon Musk has said that one of the motivations behind OpenAI was concern about the growing concentration of advanced AI technology within a small number of powerful companies.

After Google acquired DeepMind, Musk has described becoming increasingly concerned about how quickly AI capabilities were developing and whether enough attention was being given to the broader implications of increasingly powerful systems.

According to Musk, conversations with technology leaders, including Larry Page, also influenced his thinking about the future of AI.

OpenAI was subsequently established in 2015 with a nonprofit structure and an ambition to advance AI research for broad public benefit.

Over time, however, the organization evolved significantly and became one of the most influential players in the global AI industry.

This creates an interesting contrast between its original mission and its current position:

An organization partly created in response to concerns about concentrated AI power has itself become a major force shaping the direction of artificial intelligence.

China’s exports are surging, turbocharged by the artificial-intelligence boom as well as a push by Chinese companies to sell their wares abroad to escape brutal price competition at home.
